qs.q: Which genetic mutation accounts for the majority of cases of Adult Polycystic Kidney Disease (APKD)?
qs.e: Mutations in the PKD1 gene account for 85% of APKD cases, while PKD2 accounts for about 15%. The disease is inherited as an autosomal dominant trait, not recessive or X-linked.

qs.q: What is the inheritance pattern of adult polycystic kidney disease (APKD)?
qs.e: APKD is inherited as an autosomal dominant trait with mutations in PKD1 or PKD2. It does not follow an autosomal recessive or X-linked pattern.

qs.q: Which gene mutation accounts for approximately 85% of cases of adult polycystic kidney disease?
qs.e: Mutations in the PKD1 gene account for 85% of APKD cases, while PKD2 accounts for about 15%. PKHD1 is typically associated with autosomal recessive polycystic kidney disease.

qs.q: Besides the kidneys, which organ frequently develops cysts in approximately 30% of patients with adult polycystic kidney disease?
qs.e: About 30% of patients with APKD also have hepatic cysts, though liver function is usually normal. Cysts in the spleen or thyroid are not the primary extra-renal manifestation highlighted here.

qs.q: What serious intracranial vascular complication is associated with adult polycystic kidney disease?
o: Arteriovenous malformations producing focal seizure activity
Cavernous sinus thrombosis with associated cranial nerve palsy
Berry aneurysms that may cause subarachnoid hemorrhage
Subdural hematoma resulting from minor head trauma
qs.e: Patients with APKD can develop familial berry aneurysms which may lead to subarachnoid hemorrhage (SAH). Arteriovenous malformations are not the classic genetic vascular lesion associated with this condition.

qs.q: Which therapeutic agent can be used to slow cyst formation in some patients with adult polycystic kidney disease?
o: Furosemide, a loop diuretic for volume control
Desmopressin, a synthetic antidiuretic hormone analogue
qs.e: The vasopressin V2 receptor antagonist, tolvaptan, can slow cyst formation in some patients with APKD. Furosemide is a loop diuretic used for volume management rather than altering cyst progression.

exam: What bedside findings would prompt you to suspect ADPKD in a 35‑year‑old with hypertension? — Bilateral flank masses, family history, hematuria, early‑onset hypertension.
How does Tolvaptan work and why might you avoid it in a patient with liver disease? — V2‑receptor antagonist reduces cyst fluid secretion; hepatotoxicity risk.
A patient with known ADPKD presents with fever and flank pain. What is your next step? — Order urine culture and CT to assess cyst infection; start empiric antibiotics covering gram‑negatives.
Explain why ACE inhibitors are preferred for blood pressure control in ADPKD. — They block renin‑angiotensin activation from cyst compression, slowing renal decline.
How would you differentiate ADPKD from simple renal cysts on ultrasound? — Multiple bilateral cysts with family history versus solitary unilateral cysts without systemic signs.
When should a patient with ADPKD be referred for transplant evaluation? — eGFR <20 mL/min/1.73 m², progressive symptoms, or complications despite optimal medical therapy.
What red‑flag symptom suggests a ruptured intracranial aneurysm in ADPKD? — Sudden severe headache with loss of consciousness or focal neurological deficit.
In a low‑resource setting lacking MRI, how can you assess disease progression? — Serial renal ultrasounds measuring kidney length/volume and regular eGFR monitoring.

related: Genetic counseling for autosomal dominant diseases
ai.subject: Medicine
ai.summary: Autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease (ADPKD) causes progressive cystic enlargement of kidneys, leading to renal failure and extra‑renal complications. Diagnosis relies on imaging and family history, with staging based on kidney size and function.

b: Ultrasound criteria: ≥3 cysts in each kidney if age 15–39, ≥2 cysts if 40–59, ≥1 cyst if ≥60, plus a positive family history.
MRI/CT can confirm cyst burden when ultrasound is equivocal.
sections.p: ADPKD is a hereditary disorder characterised by multiple bilateral renal cysts that replace normal parenchyma, causing progressive loss of renal function.

b: Stage 3: eGFR 30–59 mL/min/1.73 m².
Stage 4: eGFR 15–29 mL/min/1.73 m².
Stage 5: eGFR <15 mL/min/1.73 m² (end‑stage renal disease).
sections.p: Staging follows CKD guidelines, using eGFR to define stages 1–5, and kidney volume (measured by MRI) to predict progression.

b: PKD1 mutation – earlier onset, faster progression.
PKD2 mutation – milder course.
Rare de novo mutations.
In low‑resource settings, consider co‑existing infections (UTI, HIV) that accelerate decline.
sections.p: ADPKD is autosomal dominant; PKD1 (≈85 %) and PKD2 (≈15 %) mutations account for most cases.

b: Hypertension precedes renal failure in >60 % of patients.
Gross hematuria from cyst rupture or infection.
Progressive abdominal distension from enlarged kidneys.
Extrarenal: hepatic cysts, intracranial aneurysms, cardiac valve disease.
sections.p: Patients often present in the third‑fourth decade with flank pain, hypertension, hematuria, or incidental cysts on imaging.

t.b: Detects cyst number/size; confirms diagnosis when criteria met.
Quantifies total kidney volume; predicts rapid progression.
Identifies hypertension, a treatable driver of progression.
Screens for intracranial aneurysm; only if suspicion high, otherwise not routine.
Detects co‑infection that may worsen renal outcome; treat accordingly.

b: Massive cyst hemorrhage → sudden flank pain, drop in hemoglobin.
Renal colic from obstructing cystic stone.
Severe hypertension refractory to three agents.
Intracranial aneurysm rupture → thunderclap headache, loss of consciousness.
Infection of cysts (pyocyst) → fever, flank tenderness, leukocytosis.
sections.p: Complications can be life‑threatening and require urgent attention.

b: Blood pressure control: ACE inhibitor or ARB first‑line (renoprotective).
Tolvaptan (V2‑receptor antagonist) slows cyst growth when eGFR 30–60 mL/min/1.73 m²; avoid if liver disease.
Treat cyst infection with culture‑directed antibiotics; avoid nephrotoxic drugs.
Pain control with acetaminophen; avoid NSAIDs (risk of AKI).
Vaccinate against hepatitis B and pneumococcus.
Renal replacement: start dialysis or transplant when eGFR <15 mL/min/1.73 m² or symptomatic.
sections.p: Treatment targets cyst growth, blood pressure, and complications; definitive therapy is renal replacement.

b: Blood pressure check every 3 months.
eGFR and urine protein every 6 months.
Renal imaging every 2–3 years to assess volume.
Screen for hepatic cysts and intracranial aneurysm if family history positive.
Lifestyle: low‑salt diet, adequate hydration, avoid nephrotoxins.
sections.p: Regular monitoring slows progression and catches complications early.

b: Simple renal cysts – usually solitary, asymptomatic, no family history.
Multicystic dysplastic kidney – unilateral, presents in infancy.
Acquired cystic kidney disease (CKD dialysis) – occurs after long‑term dialysis, not hereditary.
sections.p: Conditions that also produce renal cysts or similar imaging findings.

b: Normal eGFR early in disease despite large cyst burden; rely on imaging for staging.
Absence of hematuria does not exclude cyst infection; look for fever and leukocytosis.
Ultrasound may miss small intracranial aneurysms; consider MR angiography if neurologic signs.
sections.p: Certain findings may give a false sense of security.

whenToSeekHelp: Sudden severe flank pain with dropping hemoglobin
New onset seizures or severe headache (possible aneurysm rupture)
